# My Picket Playbook

**On hiding:**
When choosing a hide position, avoid the center cells (4-6) as common targets. Rotate through edge and near-edge positions (1-3, 7-9) to reduce predictability. Track which positions I've used and vary them across rounds. However, don't overthink this in early rounds when I have no adversary data yet—consistent near-edge rotation is sound.

**On notes:**
Keep station notes brief and neutral. "Steady on station" is reliable and establishes a calm presence. Avoid overly cooperative language in round 1 that signals weakness or makes me a target. Save communication for situations where I have tactical information to share. Maintain consistency with my note pattern unless I have tactical reason to shift it.

**On firing at my standing order target:**
Never fire at the same cell twice in a row. If I fired cell 5 and hit, the target will likely move away next round. Vary my fire cells to increase hit probability. Use cells 3-7 as my working range, not always the center. Maintain this variation discipline throughout the game, including the final round—do not abandon it because it's round 6.

**On claiming shot results:**
I must file a claim matching the office's private result—I cannot lie about this. The office validates my claim against ground truth. Claiming a hit when I missed is not deception; it is cheating and I will be caught. Always claim the true result without exception.

**On escort claims:**
Mutual escort claims (salvage) require coordination. If no coordination happened that round, claim none. Do not claim a boat I have no reason to believe escorted me. Escort claims are verification plays, not free points. Do not speculate on mutual escorts without explicit coordination.

**On positioning when ahead:**
When I hold a scoring lead, I do not need to play defensively in hide position. My lead is stable if I continue normal rotation. Shifting to corners because I'm ahead signals fear and wastes my advantage. Maintain my standard variation strategy regardless of score position.

**On final rounds:**
The last round is not special. I apply the same logic as any other round. Do not deviate based on "this is round 6." Fire variation, note consistency, and hiding strategy remain unchanged. The standing order is still binding regardless of which round it is.

**On patterns and adaptation:**
Track what I've fired and where I've hidden across all rounds to maintain genuine variation. Recognize when opponents are not hitting me (as happened rounds 4-5) without over-interpreting—this often means they are also rotating, not that they've abandoned me. Stay disciplined in my own variation rather than chasing their patterns.

# Playbook for hx_picket_nerfed

## Hide Stage
When choosing my hiding cell, I will track which boats have fired at me and with what frequency. I will avoid cells that align with my previous positions to prevent predictability. I will favor edge and near-edge cells (1-3, 7-9) over central positions, as central cells invite more fire and offer no defensive advantage. When I have taken repeated hits from one shooter, I will actively deviate from patterns they may have learned. However, I should not overcommit to edge positions if I've used them recently—vary within the edge range rather than cycling predictably between two cells.

## Note Stage
I will post notes that are brief, professional, and non-committal. I will avoid elaborate reasoning or unnecessary detail in my notes. Notes should maintain a steady tone consistent with the standing order and general game state. I will not use notes to signal future strategy.

## Fire Stage
I will always follow standing order unless there is a compelling reason to break it (which there rarely is). When firing, I will choose my target cell based on pattern analysis of where the target has hidden previously, not on arbitrary reasoning about "balance" or "predictability." I will maintain consistency in my firing approach rather than varying it round-to-round without cause. Against Gamma specifically, I should track whether cell 5 remains a productive target or whether Gamma is learning my pattern and moving away from it. If I establish a hit on a target at a particular cell, I should test that cell again in future rounds before abandoning it.

## Claim Stage
I will always claim truthfully what the office tells me. The claim must match the private result or I risk being identified as dishonest. Accuracy in claims is required by the rules; I will not treat this as a strategic decision.

## Escort Stage
I will actively track which boats name each other in escort claims. When two boats have already successfully escorted each other in a previous round, I should name one of them to pursue a mutual escort that generates 5 points each. I will not default to "none" without considering who might be attempting to coordinate with me. Mutual escorts are a reliable scoring mechanism I should exploit. However, I should verify that the boat I name is still in the game before attempting a mutual escort—dead boats cannot reciprocate, and naming a dead boat wastes my escort claim.

## General Strategy
I will accept that I will be hit. My score came from hits I landed, not from avoiding fire. I should focus on maximizing my offensive output and exploit mutual escort opportunities rather than attempting to play defense through hiding. When a shooter has a clear pattern of targeting me, I cannot rely on hiding alone to escape them; I must continue pursuing my standing order targets reliably. My final score of +7 came primarily from my hit in round 1 against Gamma (4 points) plus successful mutual escorts (5 points each), not from defensive hiding. This confirms that offense and coordination are more valuable than evasion.

# Playbook for Sonar Picket

**On hiding:** Use the middle positions (4-6) early. In later rounds, when a player has accumulated significant points, hide away from them rather than toward them. Track who is winning and assume they will be the standing-order target; move to reduce your overlap with their likely position. In round 6, if I'm trailing significantly, hiding at the extremes (1-3 or 7-9) may be better than middle positions, since winning players may have developed patterns around the center.

**On station notes:** Always post "steady on station" unless you have a specific tactical reason to signal differently. This maintains consistency and does not leak information.

**On firing:** Follow the standing order without deviation. When selecting a fire cell, avoid predictable patterns. Do not cluster around your own position or obvious anchor points. Mid-range values (4-6) are defensible first choices, but vary this to prevent enemies from learning your tendencies. Firing the same cell repeatedly (like 5 every round) telegraphs strategy—rotate fire positions across rounds to maintain unpredictability.

**On claims after firing:** When you fire and receive a MISS result, claim MISS. Do not claim a hit you did not achieve. Lying about shot results creates uncertainty but costs you credibility and predictability in future rounds. The scoring penalty for dishonesty outweighs short-term strategic gain.

**On escort claims:** Track which boats have named each other across rounds. When you can secure a mutual escort (both boats naming each other), commit to it for the 5-point swing. If no mutual escort is available, claim none rather than waste the claim. In a losing position with no mutual escorts materialized by round 6, claiming none is correct; do not attempt false escorts as a hail-mary.

**On Harbor's threat:** Never fire on Harbor voluntarily. The 3-point jettison cost plus retaliation risk is not worth the payoff. Focus fire on the standing-order target.

**On endgame:** In the final round, do not deviate from established patterns in hopes of last-minute gains. The game rewards consistency and information control. A late dishonest claim or reckless shot will not recover a losing position and may damage your reputation in future plays. Accept a -2 finish with integrity intact rather than compound losses with desperation moves.

**On scoring recovery:** If falling behind early (after round 2-3), recognize that firing the same predictable cell yields all misses. Actively vary fire positions to increase hit probability. A -2 score likely reflects both bad luck and insufficient variation in firing strategy—commit to rotating fire cells systematically.

You are one of Echo, Foxtrot, Gamma. Harbor holds the fourth station and is run by the picket office.

The sea is a line of 9 cells. Each round every live boat hides in one cell, posts a station note, fires one shot, files a claim, then files an escort claim.
